Monday. The group project on city water supply was due in five weeks, and last semester's group had fallen apart. Deepika opened the first meeting with a strange question. "How would we wreck this project? Be honest."
Harsha laughed, then answered. "Nobody knows who's doing what. We merge everything the night before. Someone stops replying."
Deepika wrote each one on the whiteboard and then turned each into a rule. Roles by name, today. Merge every Friday. A shared sheet with everyone's number and a backup email.
Friday, two weeks later. The weekly merge showed Harsha's section clashed with the map data. They fixed it in forty minutes instead of finding it at midnight.
Submission day. When one member went home for a family function and stopped answering, Deepika called the backup number from the sheet and got the final chart by noon.

Anirban, you're starting your final-year project, so let your Akash Dada tell you how ours nearly didn't happen.
Four of us, a bridge design model, three months. First meeting, our guide asked, "How could this project fail completely?" We thought it was a trick question.
Then we started. One: nobody knows whose job the calculations are. Two: all our files come together on the last day and nothing fits. Three: Rohan goes home to Siliguri and his phone doesn't work there.
Our guide said, "Good. Now fix each."
So we wrote names next to jobs. Every Saturday we combined files, even if half-done. And we made a sheet with every phone number, home landline and email.
Guess what. In week ten, Rohan did go home, and the sheet had his home number. That saved our model, beta.

Noor, you asked why I'm always telling you to aim at something. Let your Yogesh Nana tell you about his twenties.
At college I was afraid of mistakes. So I made a list of things never to do: never borrow, never take a risky course, never speak first in class, never apply where I might be rejected. I followed every rule perfectly.
Final year came. My friends had plans, a job they wanted, a subject they loved. I had no failures at all. And nothing else either. No project I cared about, no job I'd tried for, because trying meant risk.
I took the first safe clerk job that came. It took me seven years to leave it.
Avoiding the pothole is good, beti. But you also have to know where the road is going.

qa.a: He could have added one thing to aim for, like a job or subject he loved, so the rules protected a goal instead of replacing it.

qa.a: His friends may have seen him as steady but stuck, never trying for anything while they worked toward jobs and subjects they loved.

The internship portal closed at midnight, and Pradeep's hostel Wi-Fi kept dropping. He had one hour to finalise his summer plan.
He opened the document he'd been polishing for weeks. It was titled "Things to avoid". No unpaid internships. Nothing far from home. No companies with bad reviews. Nothing that needed coding, since he'd failed a coding test once. Nothing with a long application.
He scrolled the list of internships. Every single one broke at least one rule, except a data-entry role at a local office.
His friend Swati messaged: "What are you applying for?"
Pradeep stared at the screen. "Data entry. It's safe."
"Is that what you want?"
He didn't reply. At 11.58 he submitted it, then sat back feeling strangely hollow. He had avoided every risk and chosen nothing he wanted.

Mridul had inherited the weekly project meeting along with the team, and it was a mess: ninety minutes, everyone talking over each other, nobody sure what was decided. This week there was an extra problem. Half the team was on a shaky video link from the Nagpur site, and the other half was in a small room where the air conditioner roared.
Before the next meeting, Mridul tried a strange question on a notepad: how could I make this meeting even worse?
Send the agenda five minutes before. Take no notes. Let the loudest person go first. Leave the site team on mute until the end.
He looked at the first two. Those were already true.
So on Monday, the agenda went out on Friday afternoon. Vaibhav agreed to take notes on a shared screen. The meeting ended in forty minutes, and for once the site team spoke without shouting.
"Short," Vaibhav said afterwards. "And we know what we decided."

qa.a: The meeting ended in forty minutes.

qa.a: He felt a jolt of recognition and some embarrassment, seeing that his meeting already did the worst things on the list.

qa.q: What else could Mridul fix using the same list, and why?
qa.a: He could give the site team the first turn to speak, since leaving them till the end was another way to make the meeting worse.

qa.q: How does Vaibhav see the new meeting?
qa.a: Vaibhav is relieved and pleased that it was short and that everyone knows what was decided.

Vaibhav's team meetings in the Gurugram office were famous for the wrong reasons. People brought laptops and answered emails. Discussions looped. Nobody left knowing who was doing what.
On Sunday evening, he tried flipping the question. Not how to fix it, but how to make it even worse.
He wrote: share the agenda at the door. Don't write anything down. Invite everyone even if their topic isn't on it. Let it run as long as it likes.
Two of those made him wince. Agendas came late, often in the meeting itself. Notes were never taken, so Imran and others asked the same questions every week.
He changed only those two. Agenda by Thursday evening, and a rotating note-taker with a shared page.
Three weeks later, Imran stopped him in the corridor. "Meetings are half as long. And calm. What happened?"
"I made a list of how to make them worse," Vaibhav said, smiling.

First week of January. Yamini, a new team lead at the Kochi design studio, wrote her plan for the year: no missed deadlines, no client complaints, no burnt-out designers, no scope creep. She showed it to Gargi, her senior.
Gargi read it twice. "These are all things you don't want. What do you want?"
Yamini had no answer that day.
Mid-February. The team hit every deadline and had zero complaints. But they were bored, and two designers asked to switch teams. Yamini opened the plan again and saw it clearly. Every line was a wall. None of them was a road.
March. She rewrote the plan. The avoid list stayed, but above it she added one aim per month. March: launch a portfolio page. April: each designer leads one client pitch. She pinned it on the board. The two designers stayed.

Chinmay, you're saying your whole plan is just a list of don'ts. Let your Reena Masi tell you something.
When I was twenty-five and running my first clinic shift roster, I wrote rules for myself. No double shifts. No gaps at night. No nurse working three weekends running. It was a good list. Nobody could complain.

One evening I thought, where am I actually trying to go? So I added one aim each month. First month, every nurse gets one full weekend off. Next month, each senior teaches one junior a skill on shift.

I lost my pencil box AGAIN. Third time this month. Mamma was upset, and Vijay my little brother laughed.
Tonight Mamma said, "Don't just say sorry, Maria beti. Ask why."
So I asked. Why did I lose it? Because I left it at school. Why did I leave it? Because I was rushing when the bell rang. Why was I rushing? Because I only start packing AFTER the bell, and everyone is already running out.
So it's not that I'm careless. It's that I pack too late!
Tomorrow I'll start packing five minutes before the bell, when Miss says "last question". I wrote it on my hand so I don't forget.
Maria 🙂

Sarita's slate pencil box had gone missing from the village school for the second time that week. Walking home past the mustard fields, her grandfather Deepak Dada asked, "Why did it get lost?"
"I left it on the bench."
"Why?"
"I forgot it."
"Why did you forget?"
Sarita kicked a pebble. "Because the bell rang and everyone ran for the bus, so I ran too."
"And why was it still out when the bell rang?"
She stopped walking. "Because I only pack after the bell."
Dada smiled and waited.
"So if I pack before the bell," she said slowly, "I won't have to rush."
The next day, when Masterji said, "Five minutes left," Sarita put her slate, pencils and box into her cloth bag. When the bell rang, she walked out with everything.

In the small tuition room above the kirana shop in Ramgarh, Trisha's maths test came back with 38 marks. Again.
Her cousin Tarun, home from college, sat beside her. "What went wrong?"
"Silly mistakes."
"Why silly mistakes?"
She thought. "I was hurrying."
"Why hurrying?"
"The last questions were left, and ten minutes."
"Why were they left?"
Trisha flipped back to page one. The first five questions, simple equations, had taken her almost half the time. "Because I'm slow on the beginning part. I check each one three times."
Tarun nodded. "So the problem isn't silly mistakes."
"It's speed on easy questions." She grabbed her rough book. "If I practise those till they're fast, I'll have time at the end."
That week, she did twenty quick equations every evening before dinner.

Dear Jatin bhai,
You asked how I stopped getting marked late at the hostel gate every morning. The warden had warned me twice, and I was sure I just needed a louder alarm.
Then I tried asking why, properly. Why am I late? Because I can't get up at the alarm. Why? Because I'm exhausted. Why? Because I sleep at two. Why? Because I'm on my phone in bed till then. Why? Because I scroll every night without deciding to. It's a habit.
So a louder alarm was never the answer. The phone in bed was.
Now I charge my phone on the study table across the room, and I don't bring it to bed. The first three nights were hard. By the second week I was asleep by midnight.
I've been on time for eleven days straight.
Irfan

Sharmila, you want to know how your cousin Abhinav became the first one at breakfast? It's a bit embarrassing, but okay.
Second semester, I was late for the 8 a.m. lecture almost every day. My attendance was falling. I kept blaming the hostel alarm, the noisy corridor, everything.
Then one night I sat down and asked myself why five times. Late, because I oversleep. Oversleep, because I'm tired. Tired, because I sleep at 2.30. Sleep late, because I'm on my phone. On my phone, because I scroll without noticing, every night, out of habit.
The alarm was never the problem. The phone was.
So I did one simple thing. The charger went into the corridor socket outside our room, and the phone stayed there all night. My roommate thought I was mad.

passage:
I'm Raghav from Class 8. On Fridays I help in the Class 1 room.
Last week their teacher asked how to decorate for Pongal. Nandini, the smallest girl, shouted "Kolam!" first. Then everyone: "Sugarcane!" "Pots!" "Mango leaves!" "Kites!"
The teacher didn't say yes or no. She just wrote every word on the board, with little drawings.
Then she said, "Now let's pick two." Hands went up. Kolam and mango leaves won.
Nandini jumped up and down. Maybe she felt proud, but I can't say for sure. She drew a huge chalk kolam by the door.

qa.q: Which two ideas won the vote?
qa.a: Kolam and mango leaves won.

qa.q: What might Nandini's jumping up and down suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt excited and proud that her idea won, though Raghav can't say for sure.

qa.q: What else could the teacher do with the ideas that did not win?
qa.a: She could save them for the next festival, so every child's idea still feels valued.

qa.q: How might the other children see the teacher writing every word without saying yes or no?
qa.a: They may feel safe to call out any idea, since nothing was judged until the vote.

grounding: It shows young children calling out many decoration ideas, the teacher writing all of them first, and then a class vote picking two.
